text: Let's start a minute early. Good evening, everyone. I'd like to call this November 17th, 2026 meeting of the Performance Monitoring Committee to order. My name is Amy Ricardi, and I'm the chair of the committee, and I'm joined by Ms. Chandler and Ms. Chernoff. I thank everybody for being here today. I'm assuming we don't have any public comment. All right. Nope. Move right along. Okay, so item 3.01 is approval of the draft minutes of our October

6th, 2026 meeting. Have you all had a chance to review them? Are there any corrections or additions? Mm-mm. All right. Hearing none, I will entertain a motion to approve the minutes of the October 6th meeting. Go ahead. So moved. Is there a second? Second. Great. Thank you. It has been moved by Ms. Chandler and second-- No, I'm reading notes and- You're good ... thinking at the same time. It's never good doing two things at once.

It's been moved by- It's been a day ... Ms. Chandler and seconded by Ms. Schernoff. All those in favor say, "Aye." Aye. Aye. Great, and it is passed three to zero. Item 3 point-- Actually, we're on four. Item 4.01 is the Department of Academics, School Improvement and Support. It'll be presented by Dr. Ashley Ellis, our chief academic officer, and Mr. Kevin West, the director of Elementary Education and Charter Schools, and Mr.

Meisenzahl, the school improvement supervisor. Thank you all so much for being here. It's late. It feels later than it is because it's dark. I'm just glad I'm not the only one- Already ... validating. Thanksgiving. There you go. Good evening, Chair Ricardi, and the amazing Performance Monitoring Committee. So, with me, I have Mr. West from the Elementary Education Office and Mr.

Meisenzahl from the School Improvement Office. And this evening, we have lots of information to share with you based on conversations that the board has had about the school improvement process, about the way we locally identify schools for support internally, outside of rules given to us by the state and federal guidelines. We are also referencing Dr. Spence's goals for the

year that I know you all have spent a great deal of time talking with him about. And so we will do a deep dive on some of our rules for staffing schools based on their needs for different types of support. And then we'll also look at three specific schools, Forest Grove, Rolling Ridge, and Sterling Elementary, and the work that they've been doing with our central support from the Office of Elementary Ed and

all of the teams in academics to support their work towards school improvement. We'll talk about their strategies and their work underway, and then we should have plenty of time for questions. So, with that, I'll turn it over to Mr. Meisenzahl to talk a little bit about the school improvement process and identifying schools. Is it on? Thank you, Dr. Ellis. Good evening.

I'm excited to be here and thankful to have this opportunity to talk more about our school improvement process with all of you. All of our schools engage in our school improvement process based on these six core principles of improvement that are developed by the Carnegie Foundation and used widely in the school improvement process. This process centers on understanding the specific systems that create current outcomes, focusing on variations in performance, using measurable data and

disciplined inquiry to test changes like PDSA cycles, and accelerating growth by learning collaboratively as a networked community. In this initial plan phase of the Plan Do Study Act cycle, schools build a team to analyze academic, attendance, behavior, and climate data to identify key trends and determine root causes. From there, school improvement teams develop specific measurable goals

and select the research-based practices that align with the division's instructional framework for high-quality instructions. Schools do not do this alone. Central office staff provide supports to help schools develop these plans and prioritize meaningful community engagement. The do, this is where the schools put their plans into action. Collaborative learning teams drive the planning and professional development as schools implement their strategies through engaging lessons,

differentiate instruction, and provide targeted interventions, all while collecting implementation and student impact data. During the study phase, school improvement teams step back to evaluate the data collected during implementation. Throughout the year, division staff collaborate with school teams during these meetings to analyze evidence and ensure strategies effectively improve student outcomes. And finally, during the act phase, schools respond to their data

conclusions. With the continued support of division staff engaged in the process, school teams make explicit data-driven decisions to either adapt and continue a successful strategy, adopt a new strategy for the next cycle, or abandon a strategy that they're finding is having a limited impact. This ensures their continuous improvement efforts remain targeted, effective, and fully supported.

The PDSA cycle we just looked at does not happen in a vacuum. To drive student achievement, our continuous improvement process, instructional framework, and professional learning operate as one connected system. While schools are doing the hard work of analyzing root causes and implementing strategies, our instructional framework sets the shared standard for high-quality teaching in every classroom. To support this ongoing cycle, LCPS aligns division

resources and professional learning opportunities to the specific goals identified by each school improvement plan. To ensure every school receives the exact resources it needs, LCPS groups these schools into distinct levels of support. As you can see in this tiered model, this allows us to deliver targeted school improvement interventions based on identified needs across multiple data points.

While all schools receive foundational professional development, our tiered approach delivers specialized intervention exactly where it is mostly needed. So priority support is dedicated to schools with the greatest academic needs. This tier provides comprehensive support every month through a focused collaboration meeting designed to drive school-wide improvements at those schools. Enhanced support is tailored for schools with specific targeted needs.

This tier brings central office staff directly to the table during the PDSA cycle meetings, and these teams provide resources for identified strategies and actively partner with school leaders during data analysis, reflection, and decision-making for the next steps in the cycle. To sustain this work, the Departments of Academics and School Leadership meet regularly to review school data, monitor

progress, and align our resources to meet the evolving needs of our students and schools. To answer the question of exactly how schools are identified for priority or enhanced support, we utilize this identification framework. We conduct a holistic data review across four categories. We look at overall mastery and growth using SOL and MAP trends. We drill down into student reporting group gaps to ensure equity.

Beyond academics, we evaluate student engagement and readiness through discipline data, climate surveys, and chronic absenteeism data, and we weigh all of this against the school's enrollment data and staffing context. By combining this data-driven framework with hands-on division support and targeted resources, we are committed to working alongside our schools to drive continuous improvement.

So one of the first things that we look at is the staffing that's provided to schools, and I know that is of great interest to the board. So we wanted to talk a little bit about what that layered staffing approach looks like. And we tend to think about it as sort of stacked on top of each other as layers. So if you start at the bottom, all schools receive staff each year based on the board-approved division-wide staffing standards

for different staffing types. That's the baseline for all schools. And then on top of that, Title I schools or schools that have a 55% or higher percent of free and reduced lunch receive enhanced staffing that I'll go into on the next slide. That's on top of the existing division-wide staffing standards. And then another layer is the differentiated

staffing that's allocated to schools each year based, again, on their percentage of economically disadvantaged students. That staffing is managed through the Department of School Leadership. The level offices work with principals to identify needs and approve their use of differentiated staffing each year, and that can change from year to year. An additional layer that's a couple of years old and has been

widely successful is the addition of flexible staffing. And this is a pretty significant number of FTEs that are given out sort of, again, as a layer once all of these other staffing allocations are provided. The flexible staffing runs through the Department of School Leadership and the Department of Academics. So Ms. Mitchell and I review flexible staffing requests

with input from the level offices as well as the content offices based on what the position is being requested. So for example, if an additional reading specialist is requested, we would consult with the elementary office and the ELA office in teaching and learning. And then additionally, on top of that, there are central office-assigned positions, and those are typically housed in the

department's budget and assigned to a school. So for example, because we do not have instructional coaches at every school, we assign those instructional coaches based on the need. Another example might be a math resource teacher or additional reading specialists on top of what is already in the staffing standards. So a little more details. I also did want to mention that

in addition to all of these layers, there are a number of schools, 18, I believe, that fall into the class size reduction category. This is a program funded by-- We receive funds through VDOE, but we're required to keep the class sizes at those schools lower than our average class size in order to receive those funds. And so they receive additional staffing to make sure we meet the requirements of that class size reduction.

So as an example, we wanted to show you the additional staffing supports that are assigned to Title I or economically disadvantaged greater than 55% schools. So for elementary schools, you can see in that first column is the list of some of the positions. The second column is the LCPS baseline staffing standard. So all elementary schools receive this middle

column. And then in the column on the right, you'll see we have, over the past few years, been able to enhance that support for schools with a high economically disadvantaged percentage. So for example, social workers across all elementary schools are assigned at one per 2,000 students. However, we ensure that for every two Title I schools, they have a full FTE.

Additionally, you can see that family liaisons are allocated in hours using part-time funds, and we've been able to establish a standard where each school where economically disadvantaged is above 55% receives a full-time family liaison, and that support has been much appreciated by the school communities. We also know that some of our Title I

schools do receive enough funds every year to use some of those funds for staffing. That isn't widespread, I would say. As you can see here, only three schools currently have staff paid for out of Title I funds. That's for a variety of reasons. First of all, the total slice of the pie that they receive, and also they make instructional decisions each year about where to

target those Title I funds. So before I turn it over to Mr. West, I did want to just provide a little bit of context. So I think it's helpful to understand the baseline staffing, but staffing is only one piece of this really important project, this really important work of school improvement. Staffing's important, and each staff member is utilized to benefit the

students in the schools. And I also want to emphasize the importance of the work that's done in collaboration with all of the other offices that work to support the schools. And so going back to that school improvement process and that identification of schools, we have created for you a one-pager, actually, it ended up being two pages. Two-page documents, sometimes three, that really outline the

work happening in these three particular schools. These are just three examples. I do want to emphasize that all of our schools establish school improvement plans. They all have goals and strategies, and are working toward those goals and strategies. So I'm going to turn it over to Mr. West, who will give you these three examples and do a little bit deeper dive into these three schools. Thank you. Good evening.

So we're going to take an overview of a little bit more in depth of the three schools, Forest Grove, Rolling Ridge, and Sterling Elementary, and go in a little bit more depth from the slide that you have here, and also from the two-page handout that you have. For each of these, we're going to go through, first of all, what is the school profile, give some insight into the student population. Then we'll talk about the areas of needs that have been identified from performance and why they're currently in support status.

We'll also identify what are some current points of success and trending well. Then we'll get into the work that is happening this year and what the school's focus is, and how they're supporting the students in terms of reaching those proficiency this year. So as we start with Forest Grove, it serves approximately 500 students in the Sterling community. It is designated as a Title I school-wide program. Over 54% of students are English learners, and nearly

55% are economically disadvantaged. Loudoun County Public Schools has locally identified Forest Grove as a priority school to help eliminate proficiency gaps and to accelerate the academic growth with proficiency. This year, entering kindergarten at the beginning of the year, 35 out of the 60 students evaluated by VALS, the state assessment for literacy screening, were identified and placed in the

high-risk band as the school year started. Currently, within literacy overall within the school, 236 students are receiving targeted Tier 3 literacy intervention plans, and 65 students are receiving math Tier 3 plans as well. On state SOL assessments for the '25 and '26 school year, overall reading proficiency for Forest Grove was at 52%, with English learners at 30% and students with disabilities at 37.

Fall 2026 screening data shows substantial early literacy needs, particularly in foundational reading skills across the primary grades. However, demonstrates significant progress by the state performance and support framework. Forest Grove made significant growth within that last year attributed to the growth within mathematics, moving nine percentage points up to 61%, and also English language learners achieved

11.3% growth on the WIDA Access assessments, and chronic absenteeism reduced to 11%. For 2026 and '27, the school improvement plan targets a 70% proficiency on the SOL across reading, mathematics, and science. To accomplish this, the school improvement plan is going to be focusing on rigor within Tier 1 instruction, within the core instruction within the classroom.

Some of the supports to help accomplish that. The school leadership team has reengineered the master schedule this year, to assign specialized EL and special education teachers to single grade levels, which will help to provide more targeted and specialized support to students, but also provide more co-planning between teachers within those. Teachers also engaging in structured oral language routines using the QTEL

frameworks to help build academic vocabulary and language development as well. And these teams are meeting within collaborative learning teams throughout the week as well. Additionally, another aspect that's happening at Forest Grove is the EL teachers, as they're co-planning with teachers in the CLTs, are also providing professional learning on a monthly basis to help implement specific English language learner strategies within core instruction

to make sure that language development is a focus throughout the school day. So continuing on throughout the school year, there's going to be a continued focus on the collaborative co-teaching, the structured oral language routines, and then also really using the assessments that are taking place within the school to really respond to that data and really refine instruction and provide targeted support to students to try to make sure that every student is receiving the rigor,

and also that has scaffolds that they need to be successful in terms of achieving that rigor. Additionally, all teachers are engaged in job-embedded professional learning through coaching cycles that's happening from some of the resources that Dr. Ellis was mentioning before from district-level supports and staffing, and also from the school leadership team as well. And the outcomes of these coaching cycles, the success of these are directly tied to student outcomes

and assessments within the classrooms. Now we're going to take a dive into Rolling Ridge. Rolling Ridge is also a Title I school and CEP school, serving a student population where over 55% of the children are economically disadvantaged. Under state accountability, Rolling Ridge is designated as approaching expectations,

and federally is also identified as a comprehensive support and improvement school or CSI school. And so from that, it also receives a grant and funding to help support some of the priority support school work that's taking place there. 2025 and '26 performance data for Rolling Ridge demonstrates some significant challenges. On the Virginia Standards of Learning assessments, the overall reading pass rate was 52%, with English learners

at 32% and students with disabilities at 33%. In mathematics, the pass rate was at 51%, with English learners at 35% and students with disabilities with 30%. Some growth that the school and success the school had last year was within the student readiness as part of the SPSF framework. The school embarked upon targeted attendance interventions through daily student check-ins, and they were able to

reduce chronic absenteeism from a peak of 25% down to 17%, really improving the student stability and the school connections. For 2026 and '27 school year, school leadership and division teams are shifting to a targeted coaching cycle at the school focused around literacy.

So they've developed with the academic department and teaching and learning, implementing the coaching model through all the personnel available there in the school leadership team. So all teachers there are receiving coaching support focused on literacy. What they have targeted with literacy are the core actions from VDOE in terms of core action one, which focuses on interaction with text, and then they'll be moving on next to the

second core action of the questioning that goes along with the text to provide the rigor that goes along with engaging with the text. So Rolling Ridge is going to continue to really focus on growing their students and achieving proficiency of more than one year's growth through these demonstrated coaching cycles within literacy.

As we move on to Sterling Elementary School, Sterling Elementary School is also a Title I school and a priority support school serving a diverse population of about 400 students. Sixty-six percent of students identify as Hispanic, 56% are English learners, and 13% are students with disabilities, and over 92% are eligible through the Community Eligibility Provision, CEP.

The school manages 381 active MTSS support plans. Sterling Elementary is also highlighted tonight because of academic proficiency marks on the Standards of Learning assessments in 2025 and '26. Overall reading SOL pass rates stood at 57%, with English learners at 31% and students with disabilities at 26%. Math pass rates were 61% overall, with 40% proficiency

for English learners and 32% for students with disability. 2025 and '26 data also signifies significant success in terms of student growth as measured by the Virginia Accountability Framework, the SPSF, where the school was able to make significant strides based upon the student growth within the reading and math SOL assessment. Also within

the WIDA ACCESS in terms of the progress rate increasing and also reducing chronic absenteeism to 5.2%. The MAP assessments taken last year also identify growth at 52% in math and nearly 54% in reading, exceeding the standard of 50%. For this year, to focus on growth-

Sterling is focusing on increasing rigor within the classrooms, continuing to focus on oral language routines, and also they're going to be having a responsiveness to the assessment data and really making sure they're responding to that in a targeted way to support students with interventions. With the work that's taking place this year, we're also beginning to see really immediate success and dividends at Sterling Elementary on some of the

most recent common assessments within grades two and three within mathematics. Those grade levels performed above division averages. So we're excited about the work that's taking place at Sterling, and that's going to continue throughout the school year. All right, so that is a lot of information thrown at you, and we will do our best to answer your questions and would love to hear your thoughts.

Well, thank you. I'm sure this is going to be a very entertaining and interesting conversation, so thank you all for the presentation. There is a lot of data here, and since I'm the newest of the three, I have probably some more basic questions, but I would love for the two of you to start first. And I know you've got questions. I'm going to ask- Yes. ... Ms. Chandler, do you want to go first or- No, go ahead. She's like, "No, we'll let Laura do it." I appreciate that. I actually don't have too much. I'm pretty well-acquainted with the school improvement and support process and applaud the work that happens across your offices

too. Our schools vary in their needs so widely, and you all do such a great job with meeting with leadership and different teachers and teams, and making sure that these plans are catered and implemented specifically to the needs of the schools. In terms of the staffing piece, I think you're right. I think the board is keenly tuned to what is going to happen with staffing and enrollment.

So I'm feeling a little embarrassed, because I have been talking about baseline staffing, baseline staffing, baseline staffing, but I think what I really meant is baseline plus enhanced. And I've been leaving that enhanced part off, because I guess I sort of think of enhanced staffing for Title I as baseline staffing for Title I. So I need to make sure that I am communicating clearly what I mean when I say

I want to maintain baseline staffing for Title I schools. Because now I'm like, "Ah, no, I don't." I want to maintain enhanced staffing as much as we can, balancing that with the hits to the enrollment that we're seeing. So, my apologies, because for weeks on end, I have literally been saying that, and that is not the correct way to phrase this. So I'm appreciative of this presentation and being part of this, because I think that could've been lost in the process.

What I do want to ask, though, I know that the baseline staffing standards are largely driven by enrollment and also the adjustments that LCPS has had the benefit of making. Is enhanced standard Title I staffing solely in our hands based off our budget, or is that also driven by enrollment in Title I schools? So I will

first clarify that, just so we're all on the same page, the division-wide staffing standards are also in our hands, so they far exceed- Right ... the state standards of quality. So we, through the board's approval, create the division-wide staffing standards as well as the enhanced Title I staffing standards. Also, when you have said baseline over the past several weeks, I have assumed that you meant all of this. Okay, good.

But thank you for saying that out loud, and I think that makes all of us feel better as well. I might need to have a conversation with Dr. Spence too. I don't know. I've been like, "Baseline, baseline, baseline." So- I think we're all talking about the same thing. It's basically what exists already- Yes ... is kind of what I'm saying. Can we take what exists already and maneuver from there as little as possible within the budget constraints? So. Yes, because we are also not going to be recommending to you doing anything with differentiated or flexible staffing. Excellent.

That works really well and is really needed where it is. So we're not recommending any reductions in either of those as well. So to me, this is baseline. Okay. And then I forgot your question. So yes, we do have- So is enhanced driven by some kind of state, I don't want to use the word baseline again. No. Some kind of state foundation, and then we adjust with enhanced, or is enhanced solely in the division's hand, I guess, is what I-

We have taken that upon ourselves to- Okay ... use the 55% economically disadvantaged, because that's the threshold that we use to identify Title I schools, and that is our local decision. Again, it's more, generous isn't the right word, but more- Supportive ... supportive- Yeah ... than the required 75%. Is that right? No, I'm sorry, for- For identification. Yeah. 75%. Okay.

So it's much more inclusive. So we've made that local decision, and based on that local decision, that's where business and finance worked with us to include that 55% in the staffing standards. Okay. That was my understanding, so I'm glad we clarified, because- Excellent ... to me, that gives me a lot of hope for us going forward because it feels like it's more in our court in terms of where we make those decisions. Uh-oh. Do you need to say something? Go ahead. No, you're good.

Well, just to clarify, 55% is elementary. Okay. Mr. Mesenzahl reminded me 65% is secondary. Got it. So it's a little bit different at secondary. And then I would like Mr. West to explain briefly the class size reduction, because I really don't understand it, and he does. That'd be great. So on that previous chart, all those levels of staffing, those are driven by LCPS, but the one thing that we did talk about tonight, which isn't

driven by LCPS, is the VDOE class size reduction. And so the state has a formula that they send to local divisions, and based upon that formula for specific schools, they actually, at the K three level, give specific targets that a school division needs to meet. And if the school division meets those targets, then they receive funding for

that. So as a result of that, we have a lower class sizes at the K three level within those schools that's identified within that. Those generally are the same as our Title I schools, but then it usually has a little bit wider net beyond that, where we also have some schools part of class size reduction, that are also not Title I schools as well, just based upon the criteria that the state uses. Okay. I appreciate that.

So I think this is really helpful for me to understand what delineates what decision, and then as we go into budget talks, sort of thinking about what are those non-negotiables in terms of what exists now and what we want to maintain. Because even though, to me, I see this, if we can squeeze out the money, which will be the big question all budget season, but if we can, if we could maintain the staffing where it is now, if our numbers drop, that means those kids with high needs get more support. It's a simple math problem, right?

So to me, it's an opportunity if we can hold the line as much as possible to really increase support for students in the way of some, the numbers are going down, but the needs are the same. Or going up in some cases. So that's where my head space is at as we approach this, and I just want to make sure that that was clear. So I appreciate you answering that question. And then I just have one more question about the school profiles, because I kind of know the answer to this, but I want to give you a chance to tell the public and highlight.

A lot of this sounds the same. Like, "Oh, they need foundational skills and literacy," and, "Oh, they need math," and they need this. And a lot of the school profiles look and sound a lot the same. But when you get into the nitty-gritty, they're pulling different levers to get there, and the coaching supports and the staffing supports, everything is differentiated. So how do they collaborate and share with one another when they see success so that other schools can then replicate or pour into those same resources year after year?

Yeah, that's a great question and very timely because in fact, that was a big exercise that we were doing today with our elementary school principals. So, that's a big part that we talk about, where we're finding success, how can we replicate that within the school. So we talk about doing that within schools. So for instance, within a grade three at a school, if you see a certain teacher is having success with certain grade levels, how can we really grow that throughout the school? And then we also want to do the same thing where we're seeing success

from schools, how can we translate that, and replicate that across schools? So that really requires a lot of collaboration between our schools and between our principals, and really embracing what Mr. Mosenthal talks about with continuous improvement, really having that culture of learning, innovation, and growth, and collaboration from our principals and our school leadership. And it is something that they're really interested in, and they love the opportunities to do that. So for instance, today,

we identified nine schools throughout our division out of our 62 elementary schools, who were host sites. And then our principals went on learning walks there. And this actually, I was thinking today, knowing where we'd be tonight, this would be a great opportunity that I would love to do with all of you at some time as well, where there'd be an invitation to do that, where you could join in an activity like this. But where at the schools, the host principals really do what we're doing right

now and share some insight into who they are as a school, sort of the journey that they've been on, what they've been focused on, what supports and strategies and action steps that they've been taking, what then you would see in the classrooms. And then they actually go out throughout the school and visit the classrooms on these learning walks. And then based upon that, then that leads to collaborative discussion, and it's mutually beneficial. So the school hosting really gets a lot more eyes from other principals and other buildings, providing

them with feedback in terms of next steps. And then the schools that come also then have very tangible, concrete next steps then that they can take back to their own building. So that's sort of an example of when we do find success, how we can really build and grow upon that. And so... I appreciate you sharing that. And I wanted to just say that as a board member, me personally, some of the greatest things that have

come out of PMC have been when we've been able to spotlight those huge shifts in data where we see the big jumps, whether it's the belonging scores or the math scores from, I think, Freedom and Parkview, and now science. So when we get those things highlighted, even down to the elementary level, I think it's really important for us to know what's working and then to dive even a step deeper and say, "Do you have the staffing that you need? And are those things at risk because our enrollment is dropping and the budget is shifting?" So I think we're at that layered approach point, at

least for myself, to ensure that those things don't waver or falter. And so, I am appreciative of you sharing that, and I know you guys do a ton more, even at the end of the year, to make sure schools can celebrate success and really capture even the hard numbers after all of the data has been processed. So super appreciative of all you do, and I will pass it back. Thank you. Ms. Chandler. Sure. Thank you. Thank you so much for the presentation.

It is really exciting to be able to dig in and see at this level, the information that's available It is remarkable to me in reflecting on these three schools, the similarities that exist across the board, right? The size of the schools is approximate. It's close. The makeup of the schools is approximate. The challenges that the schools face, it's all very similar.

And then when you really get in and look, it's only the most minor things that are different, and yet two of these schools are off-track, and one meets expectations. And it is interesting to see the difference in the number of students who've been identified through MTSS. But in much the same way Ms. Chernov's question,

how do we harness the information that we have available to make sure that we are identifying the appropriate supports? And it is possible, right? Don't say no. No, I know. It's almost an unanswerable question. I don't really mean that. But could you help me better understand exactly how you're able

to identify what is important in this information and utilize that to identify a higher need of support? So just to clarify, talking about the data that we use to identify the different levels of support, the priority, and enhanced support? Right. Yeah. Absolutely. For us as a board member, really looking at these three comparatively and seeing how similar they are,

and noticing that there are only minor differences in the data, and yet the Virginia SPSF rating is different. And so there's obviously a difference. I just think it would be helpful to understand. That's a great question. And while we do use the SPSF data, as it is our state accountability system, what's been driving our school support is beyond the SPSF because we've identified some,

I don't want to say flaws, but some challenges, some ways that the data could be hidden. And so we've actually looked at our data through, I believe, a more rigorous model of looking at pass rates, looking at gaps for different student groups that is not part of the SPSF. We're looking at discipline data. We're looking at climate survey data. So really looking at a holistic

approach to where these schools are. We're very careful that our support system is not considered an accountability system. We already have a state and federal accountability system. But rather these schools, we use this data to identify what levels of additional support they need. I don't know if that answers your question as far as how we dig into the data further beyond the SPSF. It is helpful to contextualize the situation that we're in.

It's really just trying to look at the puzzle and understand how all the pieces fit together, and it is important to reflect on that. And I just want to add one more thing, going with what Mr. West was saying about our principals have the opportunity to collaborate, but I was just at a monthly collaborative meeting for one of our priority support schools, and they were talking about another priority support school that's doing math workshops really well.

And so how four teachers were going to be going to visit that other school to just observe and then have some debriefing with those teachers at another school on what does that look like. So we're looking to how we can leverage not only opportunities for our administrators to connect with each other, but how our teachers across schools can make those connections. It's really nice to hear that. Thank you for that. Just sort of a little bit more insight into your question as well. With the data too, you're sort of looking at proficiency marks, and across these

schools, there's a lot of similarities with that, yet schools are achieving sort of different rates with the SPSF formula, different types of things, because there's also different categories in there that look at, for instance, student growth. So for instance, Sterling Elementary last year within the student growth, they had 31% of their students within reading who achieved well over what would be one year's growth according to SOL scaled scores. So that's a pretty significant number.

That means that it was 31% of the students achieved the maximum possible value on growth as measured within the SPSF formula. And they also had within mathematics, 23% also attaining that over one year's growth, maximizing the amount of points it's possible to attain for each student within the SPSF growth formula for mathematics on the SOL as well. Thank you for that.

Well, thank you guys again. And again, I take always a different approach. Sometimes I have to always apologize for that because it is what it is.
